To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a new kinetic model for the hydrolysis of crystalline cellulose was developed that is based on the concept of a limiting surface area of the substrate and (2) this kinetic model was used to analyze the data obtained in our recent study of the effect of the enzyme concentration on the hydrolysis rate of crystalline celluloses.
the hydrolysis of lignocellulosic biomass by cellulases can be modeled by a mechanistic kinetic approach.

the hydrolysis of crystalline cellulose by cellulolytic enzymes is limited at short times by the rate of complexation of the enzymes with the insoluble cellulase substrate, while at longer times the rate is limited by the rate of decomplexation of the enzyme from the substrate, and that both of these limiting steps are independent of catalytic rate constant.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding how the properties of lignocellulosic biomass and the cellulases that degrade it influence the hydrolysis kinetics of cellulose and the overall rate of conversion of lignocelluosic biomass to fermentable sugars.
the development of new, sustainable technologies for the conversion of biomass to biofuels.

the development of a mechanistic understanding of cellulose hydro ly sis by cellulases and the application of this understanding to design of more efficient cellulase cocktails for the biofuel and bioproduct industry.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cellulose hydrolytic mechanism is not yet fully understood.

cellulases are able to bind and release from celluloses at a rate that is much faster than the rate at which they catalyze hydrolysis of the glycosidic bonds in cellulose, and that the rate of hydrolysis depends on the surface area and the DP of the cellulose.
the hydrolysis of crystalline cellulose to soluble products is a complex process, and the mechanistic details of the hydrolytic process are still being elucidated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the rate limiting step of the enzymatic cellulose degradation is the binding and dissociation of the enzyme from the cellulose substrate.
we have developed and validated the first mechanistic model that can accurately predict hydrolysis kinetics of cellulose over a wide range of conditions.

we have developed a mechanistic kinetic model for the hydrolysis of insoluble cellulose that is able to capture the initial rate, extended time course and the effects of cellulose crystallinity and particle size, as well as the effects of cellulase concentration, enzyme loadings and enzyme mixtures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cellulase catalyzed hydrolysis of insoluble cellulose is a very complex process.
the rate limiting steps for cellulose hydrolyses are still not fully understood, but that the models are getting better.
the hydrolysis of insoluble cellulose by cellulase enzymes is complex and not well understood.
